Two or three staff gowned and gloved, resternotomy set opened
items.detail: No hand-washing before closed-sleeve gloving

items.label: Bleeding / hypovolemia

items.label: Tension pneumothorax

items.label: Hypoxia

items.label: Graft or pulmonary thrombosis, obstructed valve

modes.name: Bradycardia with a pulse
modes.note: The tree follows the printed algorithm; the clock runs so the atropine interval and the record are kept.

items: Identify and treat the underlying causes
Support ABCs
Consider oxygen
12-lead ECG

support.title: Assessment and support
items: Maintain a patent airway and give oxygen
Assist breathing with positive-pressure ventilation as necessary
Attach the cardiorespiratory monitor; monitor the pulse
Establish vascular access (added by the February 2026 change notice)

treat.title: Treat
treat.text: Atropine first. If it does not work: transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Consider expert consultation and transvenous pacing; immediate pacing for unstable high-degree block when there is no access.
items: Causes: myocardial ischemia or infarction; drugs (calcium-channel blockers, β-blockers, digoxin); hypoxia; electrolytes (hyperkalemia)

q1.q: Cardiopulmonary compromise: acutely altered mental status, signs of shock or hypotension?

observe.title: No compromise
items: Identify and treat the underlying causes
Support ABCs
Consider oxygen
Consider a 12-lead ECG
Observe

support.title: Assessment and support
items: Maintain a patent airway and give oxygen
Assist breathing with positive-pressure ventilation as necessary
Attach the cardiorespiratory monitor; monitor the pulse

treat.title: Treat
treat.text: Start CPR if the heart rate stays under 60/min with compromise despite oxygenation and ventilation. IV/IO access; epinephrine; atropine for increased vagal tone or primary AV block; consider transthoracic or transvenous pacing. Check the pulse every 2 minutes: if it goes, switch to the Arrest tab.
items: Causes: hypothermia, hypoxia, toxins or medications, raised intracranial pressure, increased vagal tone, heart block, physiologic

prompts.text: Atropine may be repeated: {dose:atropine}, every 3–5 minutes, 3 mg in total.
Atropine may be repeated once: {dose:atropine} (minimum 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg).
The 2025 algorithm prints no repeat interval for epinephrine in bradycardia.

modes.name: Tachyarrhythmia with a pulse
modes.note: Unstable means the tachyarrhythmia itself is causing the compromise. Cardioversion energies are from the AHA 2025 Electrical Cardioversion algorithm.

q1.q: Heart rate typically 150/min or more. Oxygen if hypoxemic, IV access, a 12-lead ECG if available. Is the tachyarrhythmia causing hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure?

unstable.title: Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
unstable.text: Sedate whenever feasible; have oxygen, suction, an IV and intubation equipment at hand. If the rhythm is regular and narrow, adenosine may be tried first (with a central line or after heart transplant, 1 mg may be adequate). Resynchronize after each shock; if synchronization delays a critical patient, shock unsynchronized.
items: Energies: atrial fibrillation 200 J, atrial flutter 200 J, narrow-complex tachycardia 100 J, monomorphic VT 100 J; polymorphic VT: unsynchronized high-energy shock
If refractory: treat the cause, raise the energy for the next shock, add an antiarrhythmic, expert consultation

narrow.title: Stable, narrow complex
items: Vagal maneuvers, if regular
Adenosine, if regular
β-blocker or calcium-channel blocker
Expert consultation
narrow.text: Adenosine: with a central line or after heart transplant, 1 mg may be adequate. Rate control for atrial fibrillation or flutter (Part 9, Table 2): not with pre-excitation, and no calcium-channel blockers or IV β-blockers in decompensated heart failure; diltiazem and verapamil: avoid in hypotension, heart failure, cardiomyopathy and acute coronary syndromes.

wide.title: Stable, wide complex
items: Adenosine only if regular and monomorphic (central line or heart transplant: 1 mg may be adequate)
Antiarrhythmic infusion: procainamide or amiodarone (sotalol is no longer on the algorithm)
Expert consultation
No verapamil or diltiazem
Sustained polymorphic VT: unsynchronized shock; recurrent torsades with a long QT: magnesium (no 2025 dose is printed)

q1.q: Airway, oxygen, monitor, IV/IO, 12-lead ECG. Probable sinus tachycardia: normal P waves, variable R–R, infant under 220/min, child under 180/min?

sinus.title: Probable sinus tachycardia
sinus.text: Search for and treat the cause.

q2.q: Cardiopulmonary compromise: acutely altered mental status, signs of shock or hypotension?

svt-u.title: Probable SVT with compromise
svt-u.text: Adenosine if IV/IO access is already in; otherwise synchronized cardioversion. Sedate if needed, but do not delay the shock. If unresponsive to vagal maneuvers, adenosine and synchronized cardioversion and no expert is available, IV procainamide, amiodarone or sotalol may be considered; no doses are printed.

vt-u.title: Possible VT with compromise
vt-u.text: Synchronized cardioversion; expert consultation before further drugs.

svt-s.title: Probable SVT, stable
svt-s.text: Consider vagal maneuvers, then IV/IO adenosine. If no response: expert consultation.

vt-s.title: Possible VT, or SVT with aberrancy, stable
vt-s.text: If regular and monomorphic, consider adenosine. Expert consultation is recommended.

prompts.text: If needed, a second adenosine dose: {dose:adenosine}. With a central line or after heart transplant 1 mg may be enough.
If needed, a second adenosine dose: {dose:adenosine-child}.

modes.name: Anaphylaxis
modes.note: Adult doses: ICON 2019 international consensus; IM dose 500 mcg as ANZAAG, AAGBI and RCUK print it (ICON prints 300 mcg for grade II). Child IV doses: ANZAAG–ANZCA 2022 (ICON records no consensus; RCUK gives 1 mcg/kg); IM 10 mcg/kg, maximum 500 mcg (RCUK 2024). Child glucagon: ANZAAG 40 mcg/kg (max 1 mg); AHA 2025 prints 20–30 mcg/kg up to 1 mg. Sugammadex has no immediate role (ICON).

options.label: II · moderate: hypotension, tachycardia, bronchospasm, GI signs
III · life-threatening: severe hypotension, severe bronchospasm, arrhythmia

g1.title: Grade I
g1.text: Skin or mucosal signs only: no epinephrine. Remove the triggers and watch; refer for allergy testing if the urticaria or erythema is generalized.

g2.title: Grade II
g2.text: Epinephrine 20 mcg IV, then 50 mcg at 2 minutes if the response is inadequate, every 2 minutes (adult, ICON). Child under 12: 2 mcg/kg IV, increased if there is no response (ANZAAG). No IV access: IM epinephrine 500 mcg (child 10 mcg/kg, max 500 mcg). Crystalloid 500 mL rapid bolus (child 20 mL/kg), reassess, repeat.

g3.title: Grade III
g3.text: Epinephrine 50 mcg IV (100 mcg if other vasopressors have failed), then 200 mcg at 2 minutes, every 2 minutes (adult, ICON). Child under 12: 4–10 mcg/kg IV, increased if there is no response (ANZAAG). Crystalloid 1 L rapid bolus (child 20 mL/kg), repeat. Adults: start compressions if the systolic falls under 50 mmHg or there is no output, even with a rhythm (ICON, ANZAAG); ICON also advises considering compressions when ETCO₂ falls under 20 mmHg. Children: CPR for arrest or no output.

g4.title: Grade IV: cardiac or respiratory arrest
g4.text: Switch to the Arrest tab: compressions and ALS doses of epinephrine (1 mg; child 0.01 mg/kg, from the 0.1 mg/mL = 100 mcg/mL syringe). Large-volume crystalloid (ANZAAG: 2 L adult, 20 mL/kg child). ANZAAG repeats epinephrine every 1–2 minutes in adults (1–4 in children); the Arrest tab uses AHA's 3–5. Pregnant: left uterine displacement, and delivery if there is no ROSC by 4–5 minutes (ICON, ANZAAG).

groups.title: Epinephrine
groups.note: IV boluses from a 1 mg in 10 mL (100 mcg/mL) syringe for adults, 1 mg in 50 mL (20 mcg/mL) for children (ANZAAG). Repeat every 2 minutes if the response is inadequate. Grade IV uses the arrest syringe (0.1 mg/mL = 100 mcg/mL), five times as strong as the child bolus syringe.

groups.title: Fluids and refractory shock
groups.note: After 10 minutes without a sustained response: double the bolus, start the infusion after more than three boluses, add a second vasopressor (ICON).

prompts.text: Call for help, remove the triggers (the drug, chlorhexidine, colloid, latex), 100% oxygen, legs up if hypotensive; stop the procedure and lighten the anesthetic. Grade the reaction below.
Child doses are ANZAAG's, for children under 12; from 12 years use the adult doses. Each child IV dose is capped at the adult dose for the grade.
Two minutes: if the response is inadequate, repeat epinephrine {dose:ana-epi-2}.
Two minutes: if the response is inadequate, repeat epinephrine {dose:ana-epi-2}; ANZAAG: increase the dose if there is no response (grade III is 4–10 mcg/kg).
Two minutes: if the response is inadequate, repeat epinephrine {dose:ana-epi-3}.
Two minutes: if the response is inadequate, increase the dose: {dose:ana-epi-3} (ANZAAG: 4–10 mcg/kg).
IM epinephrine may be repeated every 5 minutes: {dose:ana-epi-im}.
More than three boluses: start an epinephrine infusion ({dose:ana-epi-inf}).
Ten minutes: if hypotension persists add norepinephrine or vasopressin, glucagon if β-blocked, and consider ECLS; if bronchospasm persists, inhaled or IV bronchodilators and volatile.
Send the first tryptase now (1 hour), then at 2–4 hours; a baseline sample at least 24 hours later.

items.label: Monitored for at least 6 hours
items.detail: Consider 24 hours of ICU or HDU after a severe reaction

items.label: Decided whether to proceed, cancel or postpone the surgery
Letter to the patient and the primary team
Allergy referral
items.detail: All grade II–IV reactions, and grade I with generalized urticaria or erythema

notes: Adult doses, energies and steps are the AHA 2025 algorithms and Part 9, each read in two official copies; the journal page numbers were not confirmed. Pediatric values are the AHA/AAP 2025 Part 8 text and algorithms; the Part 8 bradycardia and tachyarrhythmia sections could not be read, so those values come from the algorithms and the 2025 Highlights.

After cardiac surgery: STS 2017 expert consensus (read from the STS copy; its poster figure could not be read), AHA 2025 Part 10 and ERC 2025. No source prints a defibrillation energy for this setting; the tool shows the general adult dose. Epinephrine policy differs between STS, ERC and AHA, so the tool does not prompt it.

Anaphylaxis: the ANZAAG card values were read from extracted text and should be checked against the rendered cards; terlipressin and methylene blue: no dose appears in the sources reviewed (ICON, ANZAAG, RCUK, AHA 2025), so they are not offered. The child IV epinephrine and fluid caps at the adult dose for the grade are a safety choice, not printed values.

Not printed in the 2025 sources and so not prompted: a magnesium dose for torsades, a sotalol dose, a pediatric lidocaine maximum or repeat, a pediatric epinephrine interval in bradycardia, a pediatric atropine repeat interval, endotracheal epinephrine, pacing settings, and an ETCO₂ or diastolic pressure target in any adult recommendation.

A child's shock energy is shown capped at 200 J, the top of the adult biphasic range in the adult algorithm (120–200 J per the manufacturer): PALS gives 10 J/kg or the adult dose, whichever is lower. Pediatric amiodarone is read as 3 doses in total, the conservative reading of 'may repeat up to 3 doses'.

respAcidChronic.name: Chronic respiratory acidosis
respAcidChronic.formula: HCO₃ = 24 + 0.5 × (PaCO₂ − 40) ± 2: about 5 per 10 mmHg, derived up to PaCO₂ 70

notes: A value inside the expected band is consistent with a simple disorder but does not prove one; a value outside it means a second disorder (Adrogué and Madias 2010).

Compensation takes time: respiratory responses are acute in 5–10 minutes and chronic after 2–5 days; the response to metabolic acidosis takes 11–24 hours to complete and to metabolic alkalosis 24–36 hours. A gas drawn earlier can look mixed.
On a ventilator the ventilator sets the PaCO₂, so a respiratory component may be the settings rather than a disorder or compensation.

Winters’ formula fits best at low bicarbonate; Adrogué and Madias give PaCO₂ = 40 − 1.2 × (24 − HCO₃) ± 5 instead. For chronic respiratory acidosis the tool uses the 2018 prospective rule (0.5 per mmHg, ± 2); the 2010 rule was 0.35 per mmHg, ± 3.
In stable chronic hypercapnia the pH is often within the normal range, so a normal pH with abnormal PaCO₂ and HCO₃ is read against both bands rather than called mixed outright.

The blood gas analyzer calculates HCO₃ from pH and PaCO₂, so its own HCO₃ always agrees; a serum total CO₂ reads about 2 mEq/L higher on average. The agreement check catches typing errors and values from different samples.

Pregnancy: a normal gas (PaCO₂ about 28–32 mmHg, HCO₃ about 20) reads as a compensated respiratory alkalosis, which is the normal state in pregnancy. Infants run a lower PaCO₂ and bicarbonate than adults; these are adult rules.
Acid–base status only: the anion gap, delta ratio and osmolar gap are not part of this tool.

blocks.name: Interscalene brachial plexus block
blocks.summary: Shoulder, upper arm and, with a superficial cervical plexus block, the clavicle.
indications: Shoulder surgery
Upper arm surgery
Clavicle surgery, with a superficial cervical plexus block
coverage: Shoulder and upper arm, with the supraclavicular branches over the acromion and clavicle
Usually spares the inferior trunk (C8–T1): not a block for the hand
blocks.position: Supine, beach-chair or semi-lateral; head turned away; the patient reaches toward the knee to lower the shoulder
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–14 MHz. 5-cm 22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse 3–4 cm above the clavicle over the external jugular vein, tilted slightly caudad. C5–C7 roots lie as round hypoechoic dots between the anterior and middle scalene. Needle in plane, usually lateral to medial, aimed between the roots, never at one
volume: 7–15 mL (NYSORA ultrasound page); the older landmark chapter gives 15–20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5–0.75%
Catheter: 4–5 mL through the needle, then advance 2–3 cm; ropivacaine 0.2% 5 mL/h with a 5 mL bolus every 60 min (landmark chapter)
blocks.onset: Ropivacaine 0.5%: onset 15–20 min, anesthesia 6–8 h, analgesia 8–12 h; 0.75%: 5–15 min, 8–10 h, 12–18 h (landmark chapter table)
cautions: Hemidiaphragmatic paresis is common (possibly near 100% in the landmark chapter): caution with lung disease; contralateral phrenic or recurrent laryngeal palsy is a relative contraindication
Horner syndrome; hoarseness in 10–20%
Vertebral artery and thyrocervical branches nearby: color Doppler before inserting, aspirate before injecting
Stop if opening pressure exceeds 15 psi or the patient reports severe pain: intraneural injection can track toward the spinal canal
tips: Phrenic-sparing options NYSORA lists: lower volume, a more caudad injection (around C7), a supraclavicular or a suprascapular block
Lateral-to-medial needle path keeps away from the phrenic nerve on the anterior scalene
After 5–7 mL, trace the plexus down to the supraclavicular fossa to check the spread

art.caption: Transverse view at C6: the C5–C7 roots stacked between the anterior and middle scalene.

blocks.name: Supraclavicular brachial plexus block
blocks.summary: Arm, elbow, forearm and hand; shoulder possible.
indications: Arm, elbow, forearm and hand surgery
Shoulder surgery is also possible (ultrasound page; the landmark chapter says below the shoulder)
coverage: Upper limb, often including the shoulder
Never the medial upper arm skin (intercostobrachial, T2): add a subcutaneous injection just below the axilla
The deep medial contingent (C8–T1) must be reached for the hand and medial forearm
blocks.position: Supine, semi-sitting or slightly tilted; head turned away; reaching for the knee lowers the clavicle
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–18 MHz. 5-cm 22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse just above the clavicle, slightly lateral of its midpoint, tilted caudally. The plexus is a cluster of hypoechoic nodules posterior and lateral to the subclavian artery, on the first rib above the pleura, usually 1–3 cm deep. Needle in plane, lateral to medial, into the sheath behind the artery
volume: 20–25 mL (ultrasound page; less suggested for older patients); the landmark chapter gives 30 mL of mepivacaine 1.5% with epinephrine
Catheter: ropivacaine 0.2% or bupivacaine 0.125% at 5–8 mL/h with 3–5 mL hourly boluses
blocks.onset: Mepivacaine 1.5% with epinephrine: about 3–4 h of anesthesia (2–3 h without); ropivacaine, levobupivacaine or bupivacaine 5–7 h (landmark chapter)
cautions: Very vascular: subclavian, dorsal scapular, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries; color Doppler first
Pneumothorax is rare and often delayed: keep the needle tip in view
Phrenic palsy is less likely than after interscalene but not avoidable (about 50% in the landmark chapter); axillary or infraclavicular if a 27–30% fall in lung function is not tolerable
Do not inject against an opening pressure above 15 psi
tips: Insert no deeper than about 1 cm at first and hydrolocate as you advance
The dorsal scapular artery often runs near or through the plexus: sweep with color Doppler

art.caption: Transverse view above the clavicle: the plexus lateral to the subclavian artery, the first rib and pleura beneath.

blocks.name: Infraclavicular brachial plexus block
blocks.summary: Arm below the shoulder, elbow, forearm and hand; well suited to catheters.
indications: Arm, elbow, forearm and hand surgery
Arteriovenous fistula surgery (landmark chapter)
coverage: Upper limb below the shoulder (the cords)
The medial upper arm skin (intercostobrachial) may need a separate subcutaneous injection
blocks.position: Supine, head turned away, arm abducted to 90° with the elbow flexed
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–14 MHz. 8–10 cm 21–22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe parasagittal just medial to the coracoid, below the clavicle and lateral to the pleura. The axillary artery lies deep to pectoralis major and minor, the vein medially, the cords around the artery. Needle in plane from the cephalad end, steeply to the posterior aspect of the artery; aim for U-shaped spread around it
volume: 20–30 mL in adults, in two or three aliquots (ultrasound page); 30 mL in the landmark chapter
Catheter: 5 mL/h with 8 mL hourly boluses
blocks.onset: Landmark chapter: short-acting agents last 1.5–3 h, intermediate 4–5 h, long-acting (bupivacaine 0.25–0.5%, ropivacaine 0.5%) 10–14 h
cautions: Pneumothorax: keep the probe and the needle path lateral to the chest wall and pleura
Aspirate about every 5 mL
Do not inject against more than 15 psi
Catheters left over 72 h had the highest infection rate in a registry (Kubulus 2024)
tips: An acoustic artifact deep to the artery is often mistaken for the posterior cord
A 'heel-up' probe tilt flattens the needle angle
Seeing every cord is not needed for success

art.caption: Parasagittal view below the clavicle: the cords around the axillary artery, deep to both pectoral muscles.

blocks.name: Axillary brachial plexus block
blocks.summary: Elbow, forearm and hand, far from the pleura and phrenic nerve.
indications: Elbow, forearm and hand surgery
Moderate to long forearm, wrist or hand surgery, with or without an arm tourniquet (landmark chapter)
coverage: From mid-arm to the hand
Spares the deltoid skin (axillary nerve) and the medial upper arm (intercostobrachial: add a subcutaneous injection)
The musculocutaneous nerve needs its own injection unless it leaves the median nerve distally (16%)
blocks.position: Supine, arm abducted to 90°; avoid over-abduction
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–14 MHz, light pressure so the veins stay visible. 5-cm 22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe short-axis on the medial arm just distal to the pectoralis major insertion. Median, ulnar and radial nerves sit around the axillary artery; the musculocutaneous nerve lies in or between biceps and coracobrachialis. Needle in plane from the biceps side: first behind the artery (radial), then median and ulnar, then the musculocutaneous nerve. A single injection deep to the artery is an accepted alternative
volume: 15–20 mL (20 mL is usually adequate in an adult): radial 5–7 mL, median and ulnar a further 7–10 mL, musculocutaneous 5–7 mL (ultrasound page); 5–10 mL per nerve in the landmark chapter
Catheter: ropivacaine 0.2% at 0.1 mL/kg/h, 5–10 mL/h (landmark chapter)
blocks.onset: Landmark chapter: onset 10–20 min (15–20 min for ropivacaine or bupivacaine); anesthesia 3–4 h with short- or intermediate-acting agents, 6–16 h with ropivacaine or bupivacaine
cautions: Intravascular injection: aspirate often and inject slowly; toxicity has followed apparently easy blocks
Too much probe pressure hides the veins and invites venous puncture; no visible spread may mean a vein
Registry: more block failures and postoperative nerve dysfunction than interscalene (Kubulus et al.)
tips: An enhancement artifact deep to the artery is often mistaken for the radial nerve
Prescan for the musculocutaneous nerve with small proximal-distal slides

art.caption: Short-axis view on the medial arm: median, ulnar and radial nerves around the axillary artery; musculocutaneous in coracobrachialis.

blocks.name: Wrist block
blocks.summary: Hand and finger surgery without an arm block.
indications: Hand and finger surgery
coverage: The whole hand except the territory of the deep branch of the radial nerve
No forearm or arm anesthesia: an upper-arm tourniquet is not covered
blocks.position: Supine, arm volar side up
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–14 MHz. 22–25-gauge needle with low-volume tubing
blocks.target: Each nerve blocked 5–10 cm above the wrist crease with the probe transverse: the median nerve between the flexors in the mid-forearm, the ulnar nerve beside the ulnar artery under flexor carpi ulnaris, the superficial radial nerve by infiltration over the radial styloid or beside the radial artery
volume: 3–4 mL per nerve, 10–15 mL in all
cautions: The ulnar and radial nerves lie beside their arteries: arterial puncture can cause a hematoma
tips: Slide the probe up and down to tell the median nerve from tendons
Follow the ulnar artery to find the ulnar nerve

art.caption: Transverse view of the mid-forearm: the median nerve between the superficial and deep flexors.

blocks.name: Superficial cervical plexus block
blocks.summary: Skin of the neck and over the clavicle: carotid, superficial neck and, with interscalene, clavicle surgery.
indications: Carotid endarterectomy
Superficial neck surgery
Thyroidectomy, clavicle surgery, cervical spine procedures and central venous access analgesia (Jarvis review, NYSORA clinical update)
coverage: Lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves: the anterolateral neck, around the ear and the skin over and below the clavicle
Not the face; not the deep neck structures
blocks.position: Supine or semi-sitting, head turned slightly away
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–18 MHz. 5-cm 23–25-gauge needle with low-volume tubing
blocks.target: Probe transverse over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at its midpoint (about the cricoid). Inject under the posterior edge of the muscle, above the prevertebral fascia (intermediate block); the plexus need not be seen
volume: 5–15 mL (the page's goal section says 5–10 mL); about 10 mL deep to the SCM is reliable
Ropivacaine 0.25–0.5%, bupivacaine 0.25% or lidocaine 1%
cautions: Stay superficial to the prevertebral fascia: the deep block risks vertebral artery and intrathecal injection, and phrenic and recurrent laryngeal palsy
Aspirate, then give 1–2 mL to confirm the spread
tips: Have the patient lift the head to find the posterior border of the SCM

art.caption: Transverse view at the SCM midpoint: inject under its posterior edge, above the prevertebral fascia.

blocks.name: Suprascapular nerve block
blocks.summary: Shoulder pain; a phrenic-sparing option for shoulder surgery.
indications: Acute and chronic shoulder pain: frozen shoulder, rotator cuff tear, glenohumeral arthritis
A phrenic-sparing alternative to interscalene for shoulder surgery (NYSORA interscalene page)
coverage: NYSORA's free pages do not state the coverage or whether an axillary nerve block should be added
blocks.position: Not stated on NYSORA's free page (sitting is usual for a posterior approach)
blocks.equipment: Probe coronal over the supraspinous fossa (type not stated on the free page)
blocks.target: Probe coronal over the supraspinous fossa, tilted slightly forward. The nerve and suprascapular artery lie on the floor of the fossa under the supraspinatus fascia, between the suprascapular and spinoglenoid notches. Needle in plane from the medial end of the probe to the fossa floor
volume: 5–8 mL
cautions: The suprascapular artery runs with the nerve: watch for it
NYSORA's free page lists no complications; pneumothorax and arterial puncture are not discussed

art.caption: Coronal view of the supraspinous fossa: nerve and artery on the bony floor under supraspinatus.

blocks.name: Femoral nerve block
blocks.summary: Anterior thigh, femur, patella and knee; hip fracture analgesia.
indications: Femur, patella, quadriceps tendon and knee surgery
Analgesia for hip fracture
coverage: Anterior and medial thigh to the knee, and a strip of the medial leg and foot (saphenous); articular branches to hip, knee and ankle
blocks.position: Supine, table flat; tape an obese pannus away
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–18 MHz. 50–100 mm 22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse on the femoral crease over the pulse (slide proximally if the deep femoral artery appears). The nerve is hyperechoic, 2–4 cm deep, on the iliopsoas lateral to the artery and deep to the fascia iliaca. Needle in plane lateral to medial to the lateral edge of the nerve; circumferential spread is not needed
volume: 10–15 mL (ultrasound page); 15–20 mL in the landmark chapter and 20 mL in NYSORA's pain chapter
Catheter: ropivacaine 0.2% 5 mL/h with a 5 mL bolus every 60 min
blocks.onset: Landmark chapter: onset 10–30 min by agent; anesthesia 1–15 h, analgesia 2–30 h
cautions: Quadriceps weakness: no safe weight-bearing on that leg; a knee immobilizer for walking reduces falls (landmark chapter)
The femoral vein collapses under the probe: release pressure and recheck before injecting
Injecting above the fascia iliaca fails
tips: A pool at the posterolateral or anterior surface of the nerve is enough
For catheters, start laterally so more catheter lies in the iliacus

art.caption: Transverse view at the femoral crease: the nerve lateral to the artery, under the fascia iliaca.

blocks.name: Fascia iliaca block
blocks.summary: Femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves from one injection under the fascia iliaca.
indications: Anterior thigh and knee surgery
Analgesia after hip and knee procedures
coverage: Femoral nerve in all cases, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in 80–100%
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve may be missed
blocks.position: Supine, table flat
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 6–14 MHz. 80–100 mm 22-gauge needle, short bevel to feel the fascial 'pop'
blocks.target: Infrainguinal: probe transverse just below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery, at about a third of the way from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle; needle in plane under the fascia iliaca, aiming for spread medially to the femoral nerve and laterally under sartorius. Suprainguinal: probe sagittal above the ligament over the iliacus, tip just deep to the fascia iliaca
volume: Adults 20–40 mL (the page's tips say 30–40 mL); children 0.7 mL/kg
Ropivacaine 0.2%
cautions: Injectate that pools instead of layering out means the wrong plane: stop and reposition
NYSORA's page lists no complications; large volumes add to the total local anesthetic dose
tips: Find the femoral artery first; tilt the probe while pressing to bring out the fascia iliaca
Success is best predicted by spread to the femoral nerve medially and under sartorius laterally

art.caption: Infrainguinal view: local anesthetic spreading under the fascia iliaca toward the femoral nerve.

blocks.name: PENG block (pericapsular nerve group)
blocks.summary: Hip fracture analgesia aimed at the anterior hip capsule, sparing motor function.
indications: Hip fracture analgesia (the trial NYSORA summarizes)
Anterior hip capsule pain where motor sparing matters
coverage: Articular branches to the anterior hip capsule
Lateral thigh coverage was better with a suprainguinal fascia iliaca block (NYSORA news)
blocks.position: Not on NYSORA's free pages (supine)
blocks.equipment: Not on NYSORA's free pages: the full technique is in its subscription content
blocks.target: The plane between the psoas tendon and the anterior hip capsule near the iliopubic eminence; needle in plane, lateral to medial, deep to the psoas tendon
volume: 20 mL of ropivacaine 0.3% in the trial NYSORA summarizes (a trial dose, not a NYSORA recommendation)
blocks.onset: In that trial, dynamic pain fell about 3 points by 30 minutes
cautions: NYSORA's free pages list no complications; motor function was preserved in the trial

art.caption: Oblique view along the superior pubic ramus: injection deep to the psoas tendon, on the bone.

blocks.name: Adductor canal (saphenous) block
blocks.summary: Knee analgesia that largely spares the quadriceps; the saphenous nerve for medial leg and ankle.
indications: Knee surgery analgesia, knee arthroplasty included
With a sciatic block for medial foot and ankle surgery
Saphenous vein stripping or harvest
coverage: Skin of the medial leg and foot (saphenous, purely sensory)
Motor sparing in intent; a large or proximal injection can partly block vastus medialis
blocks.position: Supine, thigh abducted and externally rotated
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–14 MHz. 80 mm 22–25-gauge needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse on the anteromedial thigh at the junction of the middle and distal thirds. The saphenous nerve lies beside the femoral artery under sartorius, between vastus medialis and the adductors. Needle in plane lateral to medial, tip under sartorius beside the artery
volume: Saphenous 5–10 mL; adductor canal up to 20 mL
Trial: 10 mL of bupivacaine 0.15% was non-inferior to 20 mL of 0.25%
cautions: Partial quadriceps weakness with proximal or large injections: assist walking
Avoid the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery (color Doppler)
tips: Block as distally as practical to limit motor spread
Seeing the nerve is not needed: 5–10 mL beside the artery under sartorius should suffice
NYSORA pages differ on which side of the artery to inject (lateral and anterior on the technique page, medial in the pain chapter)

art.caption: Transverse view of the mid-distal thigh: the saphenous nerve beside the femoral artery under sartorius.

blocks.name: IPACK block
blocks.summary: Posterior knee pain after arthroplasty or ACL repair, without foot drop.
indications: Posterior knee pain after knee arthroplasty, with a femoral or adductor canal block
Posterior knee pain after ACL reconstruction
coverage: Articular branches to the posterior knee capsule (popliteal plexus, obturator)
Avoids the tibial and common peroneal motor branches: no foot drop
blocks.position: Not on NYSORA's free pages
blocks.equipment: Not on NYSORA's free pages
blocks.target: Probe transverse over the medial knee 2–3 cm above the patella, slid until the distal femoral shaft and the popliteal artery are both in view; needle in plane from the anteromedial knee into the space between the artery and the femur (posterior capsule)
volume: 15–20 mL (three-step technique on NYSORA's tips pages); 20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% in a knee arthroplasty trial
cautions: Identify the popliteal artery before advancing; NYSORA's free pages list no complications
tips: Combine with an adductor canal or femoral triangle block for the front of the knee

art.caption: Transverse view above the knee: injection between the popliteal artery and the femur.

blocks.name: Popliteal sciatic nerve block
blocks.summary: Foot, ankle and Achilles surgery; add a saphenous block for the medial side.
indications: Foot, ankle and Achilles tendon surgery
Allows a calf tourniquet (landmark chapter)
coverage: Below the knee: tibial and common peroneal territories, and fibers to the posterior knee joint
Not the medial leg and foot (saphenous): add a saphenous or adductor canal block
blocks.position: Lateral approach: supine with the foot on a raised rest. Posterior approach: prone or lateral
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–12 MHz. 50–100 mm 21–22-gauge short-bevel insulated needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse in the popliteal fossa, slid up from the crease to where the tibial and common peroneal nerves diverge (usually 5–10 cm above the crease), lateral and superficial to the popliteal vessels between biceps femoris and semimembranosus. Lateral approach: needle in plane horizontally from the lateral thigh into the common sheath
volume: 15–20 mL (ultrasound page); 20 mL in the landmark chapter
Catheter: ropivacaine 0.2% 5 mL/h with a 5 mL bolus every 60 min
blocks.onset: Landmark chapter: onset 10–30 min by agent; anesthesia 1–15 h, analgesia 2–30 h
cautions: Never inject against pressure above 15 psi
Protect the anesthetized heel from pressure necrosis
Sciatic block impairs walking
tips: Ask the patient to dorsiflex and plantarflex: the two divisions move against each other
Enter the skin 2–3 cm lateral to the probe to flatten the needle

art.caption: Transverse view above the popliteal crease: the tibial and common peroneal nerves diverging, lateral to the vessels.

blocks.name: Ankle block
blocks.summary: Forefoot and toe surgery with no calf weakness: five nerves at the ankle.
indications: Distal foot and toe surgery
Midfoot and forefoot anesthesia and analgesia without motor block
coverage: Tibial: heel and sole. Deep peroneal: first web space and ankle joint. Superficial peroneal: dorsum. Sural: lateral foot. Saphenous: medial malleolus (may be omitted for forefoot surgery)
blocks.position: Supine, pillow under the calf; the leg rotated as needed
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 8–18 MHz. 22–25-gauge needle with low-volume tubing
blocks.target: Tibial: just behind the posterior tibial artery at the medial malleolus. Deep peroneal: lateral to the anterior tibial artery at the extensor retinaculum. Superficial peroneal: 5–10 cm above the lateral malleolus, above the fascia. Sural: beside the small saphenous vein. Saphenous: beside the great saphenous vein
volume: 3–5 mL per nerve (ultrasound page)

Landmark chapter: 5 mL each for the deep nerves and a 10–15 mL subcutaneous ring for the superficial ones; usually under 30 mL in all. Lidocaine 2% for short cases, ropivacaine 0.5% for long or painful ones
blocks.onset: Give long-acting blocks at least 20, ideally 30 minutes before incision (landmark chapter)
cautions: Avoid epinephrine at the ankle, above all with peripheral vascular disease (if used, 1:300,000 or weaker)
Tendons mimic the tibial nerve: trace them proximally
Stay alert to compartment syndrome
tips: If the superficial nerves cannot be seen, infiltrate a subcutaneous ring
Color Doppler finds the posterior and anterior tibial arteries that the deep nerves sit beside

art.caption: Transverse view at the medial malleolus: the tibial nerve just behind the posterior tibial artery.

blocks.name: Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block
blocks.summary: Somatic analgesia of the anterior abdominal wall; lateral or subcostal.
indications: Abdominal wall and parietal peritoneum analgesia: bowel resection, appendectomy, cholecystectomy, cesarean delivery, abdominal hysterectomy, laparotomy
Subcostal approach for upper abdominal incisions
coverage: The segments reached, lower thoracic to L1
Lateral TAP does not reliably reach above T10; subcostal does not cover the lateral wall; no visceral analgesia
blocks.position: Supine (truncal chapter) or lateral, block side up
blocks.equipment: Linear probe (curved in very obese patients). 50–100 mm 20–22-gauge needle; a blunt tip helps feel the planes
blocks.target: Lateral: probe transverse at the midaxillary line between the costal margin and iliac crest; needle in plane until local anesthetic opens the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis as a lens, not swelling the muscle. Subcostal: probe along the costal margin near the midline; plane between the posterior rectus sheath and transversus abdominis
volume: At least 15 mL per block (technique page); 20–30 mL of ropivacaine 0.25% per side (truncal chapter); children 0.4 mL/kg per side
Dose to the patient's size, above all when bilateral
blocks.onset: A single shot is short-lived and rebound pain can follow (2025 NYSORA update)
cautions: Bilateral blocks approach the maximum safe dose: calculate the total
Muscle swelling instead of plane separation means an intramuscular tip: move 1–2 mm
Peritoneum and bowel lie just deep to transversus abdominis
tips: Enter the skin a few centimeters from the probe to keep the needle visible
Saline or chloroprocaine hydrodissection spares long-acting local anesthetic when combining bilateral TAP and rectus sheath blocks

art.caption: Transverse view of the lateral abdominal wall: a lens of local anesthetic between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

blocks.name: Rectus sheath block
blocks.summary: Midline and umbilical incisions, done on both sides.
indications: Umbilical hernia repair and other umbilical surgery
Open abdominal surgery through a midline incision, bilaterally
coverage: Periumbilical and anteromedial abdominal wall, T9–T11
Not the lateral wall or the viscera
blocks.position: Supine
blocks.equipment: Linear probe. 50–100 mm 22-gauge short-bevel needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse just lateral to (or 1 cm above and lateral to) the umbilicus over the rectus; needle in plane through the anterior sheath and rectus to rest on the posterior sheath (out-of-plane is often easier in obese patients). Find the epigastric arteries with color Doppler
volume: 10 mL per side, e.g. ropivacaine 0.5% (truncal chapter); 10–15 mL per side of 0.375–0.5% (four-step page); children 0.1 mL/kg per side
cautions: Aspirate and give a 1–2 mL test dose
Both sides add to the total dose, more so with TAP blocks

art.caption: Transverse view beside the umbilicus: local anesthetic between the rectus and the posterior sheath.

blocks.name: Quadratus lumborum block
blocks.summary: Abdominal surgery below (QL1) or above and below the umbilicus (posterior and transmuscular).
indications: Abdominal surgery below the umbilicus (lateral QL1)
Incisions up to T6, above or below the umbilicus (posterior QL2, transmuscular QL3)
coverage: By variant: L1 (QL1) up to T4–L1 with some visceral analgesia (transmuscular)
The transmuscular approach can spread to the lumbar plexus and weaken the leg
blocks.position: Lateral decubitus preferred
blocks.equipment: Low-frequency curved probe (2–5 MHz). 22-gauge short-bevel needle
blocks.target: Probe transverse on the flank above the iliac crest at about L4. Transmuscular: the 'shamrock' (L4 transverse process as the stem; erector spinae, quadratus lumborum and psoas as the leaves); needle in plane from posterior to anterior through QL to the QL–psoas plane. QL1: lateral edge of QL. QL2: its posterior surface
volume: NYSORA says only that QL blocks need large volumes; it gives no figure
This region is vascular: dose for the patient's size, above all when bilateral
cautions: Kidney, liver or spleen puncture: always see the kidney (its lower pole can reach L4 in deep inspiration)
Leg weakness from lumbar plexus spread (transmuscular)
Lumbar arteries behind QL: color Doppler first
tips: Use the shamrock at L4 to orient the transmuscular approach

art.caption: Transverse flank view at L4 (the 'shamrock'): transmuscular injection between quadratus lumborum and psoas.

blocks.name: Erector spinae plane (ESP) block
blocks.summary: Rib fractures and back and chest wall surgery; spreads over several levels.
indications: Rib fractures, back and chest wall surgery (NYSORA tips page)
Its clear indications are still not well defined (NYSORA main page)
coverage: Spreads up and down several levels deep to the erector spinae, mainly to the dorsal rami; spread into the paravertebral space is debated
blocks.position: Not stated on NYSORA's free pages (sitting, lateral or prone)
blocks.equipment: Not stated on NYSORA's free pages
blocks.target: Probe paramedian sagittal about 2 cm from the midline over the transverse processes (example T5). Above T5, trapezius, rhomboid major and erector spinae lie superficial; the pleura should not be visible. Needle in plane, cranial to caudal, to bone contact on the transverse process
volume: 1–3 mL test, then 20–30 mL
cautions: NYSORA's free pages list no complications
Pleura visible means too lateral (over the ribs): slide medially
tips: Laminae (flat lines) mean too medial; rounded ribs with pleura between them mean too lateral
Confirm every muscle layer and the transverse process before injecting

art.caption: Parasagittal view at T5: local anesthetic spreading under the erector spinae over the transverse processes.

blocks.name: Ilioinguinal–iliohypogastric block
blocks.summary: Inguinal hernia repair and other groin or suprapubic incisions.
indications: Anesthesia and analgesia for inguinal hernia repair and other inguinal surgery
Analgesia after a suprapubic incision
coverage: The groin (L1)
blocks.position: Supine
blocks.equipment: Linear probe. 50–100 mm 21–22-gauge needle
blocks.target: Probe oblique just medial to the ASIS on the line to the umbilicus: three muscle layers with the iliac bone shadow laterally. The nerves are hypoechoic ovals between internal oblique and transversus abdominis; the deep circumflex iliac artery runs in the same plane
volume: Adults 10 mL per side; children 0.15 mL/kg per side of ropivacaine 0.5%
cautions: NYSORA's page lists no complications (femoral nerve spread and bowel puncture are not discussed)
tips: Color Doppler finds the deep circumflex iliac artery beside the nerves
Out-of-plane with small boluses may be easier in obese patients

art.caption: Oblique view medial to the ASIS: the two nerves between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

blocks.name: PECS I and II blocks
blocks.summary: Breast surgery: pectoral muscles (PECS I), adding the lateral chest wall and axilla (PECS II).
indications: Breast surgery; PECS II for mastectomy and resections involving the pectorals, serratus or axilla
Pacemaker insertion (PECS I)
coverage: PECS I: pectoral muscles (medial and lateral pectoral nerves)
PECS II adds the lateral chest wall and axilla (lateral branches of T2–T4, long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves)
The anterior chest wall (anterior branches of T2–T4) cannot be guaranteed
blocks.position: Supine, arm beside the chest or abducted 90°
blocks.equipment: Probe and needle not stated for PECS on NYSORA's page
blocks.target: PECS I: probe below the lateral clavicle near the coracoid, rotated obliquely; the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery marks the plane between pectoralis major and minor (1–3 cm deep). PECS II: slide laterally to the 3rd–4th rib at the anterior axillary line; the second injection goes between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior (3–6 cm deep)
volume: 0.2 mL/kg of long-acting local anesthetic per injection; study examples 10 mL (PECS I) and 20–25 mL (PECS II)
Bupivacaine 0.25%, levobupivacaine 0.15–0.25% or ropivacaine 0.375–0.5% in the studies cited
blocks.onset: One study: 4.9 h of analgesia with PECS II against 3.3 h with paravertebral
cautions: Find the thoracoacromial artery's pectoral branch before injecting
NYSORA's page lists no complications for PECS
tips: Confirm each plane with hydrodissection
NYSORA pages place the second PECS II injection at the 4th or the 3rd rib

art.caption: Oblique view over the upper ribs: PECS I between the pectorals, PECS II between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior.

blocks.name: Serratus anterior plane block
blocks.summary: Lateral chest wall: thoracotomy, rib fractures, mastectomy, thoracoscopy.
indications: Thoracotomy and rib fractures (case reports)
Mastectomy, thoracoscopic lung resection (studies cited)
Not supported for sternotomy
coverage: Lateral hemithorax: lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves (about T3–T9), intercostobrachial, long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves
Not the anterior chest wall or sternum
blocks.position: Lateral, block side up, or supine with the arm brought forward
blocks.equipment: Linear probe, 6–13 MHz. 50–100 mm 22-gauge needle
blocks.target: Count ribs down to the 4th–5th at the midaxillary line; probe coronal, tilted posteriorly (or across the axilla to see the thoracodorsal artery). Inject either between latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior (superficial) or under serratus on the rib (deep)
volume: 0.4 mL/kg of long-acting local anesthetic; study examples 30 mL bupivacaine 0.25%, or 20 mL 0.125% then an infusion
blocks.onset: Volunteers (superficial injection): paresthesia lasted about 12.5 hours
cautions: Pneumothorax was reported with continuous serratus catheters after cardiac surgery
Lower injection pressures and tailored volumes are suggested
tips: The thoracodorsal artery lies on serratus: a good landmark for the superficial plane

art.caption: Coronal view over the 4th–5th ribs: the superficial plane between latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior.

blocks.name: Thoracic paravertebral block
blocks.summary: One-sided somatic and sympathetic block over several thoracic levels.
indications: Unilateral pain of thoracic or abdominal origin
Breast surgery and inguinal hernia repair (ultrasound chapter)
Thoracotomy, VATS, rib fractures, cholecystectomy (landmark chapter, NYSORA update)
coverage: Several contiguous dermatomes on one side, somatic and sympathetic
Contralateral spread in about 10% after a single injection (landmark chapter)
blocks.position: Sitting preferred; lateral, block side up; or prone
blocks.equipment: High-frequency linear (author's choice) or curved probe, depth 4–6 cm. 22-gauge Tuohy for a single shot, 16–18-gauge for catheters (landmark chapter)
blocks.target: The wedge between the parietal pleura, the internal intercostal membrane and the vertebra, beside the transverse process. Ultrasound: transverse or paramedian sagittal oblique scans, or an intercostal approach in plane lateral to medial; a 2–3 mL saline test bolus should push the pleura down. Landmark: walk off the transverse process no more than 1.5 cm
volume: Single injection 20–25 mL in aliquots, or 3–5 mL per level for multiple injections (landmark chapter; the ultrasound chapter gives none)
Bupivacaine, levobupivacaine or ropivacaine 0.5% with epinephrine 2.5–5 mcg/mL; breast surgery example ropivacaine 2 mg/kg diluted to 20 mL
Catheter: bupivacaine 0.25% or ropivacaine 0.2% at 0.1–0.2 mL/kg/h
blocks.onset: Thoracic: anesthesia 3–4 h, analgesia 8–18 h (landmark chapter)
cautions: Landmark chapter: vascular puncture 3.8%, hypotension 4.6%, pleural puncture 1.1%, pneumothorax 0.5%; 5% pleural puncture in a cadaver ultrasound study
Never more than 1.5 cm past the transverse process; avoid medial needle angles (epidural or intrathecal spread)
Contraindications: infection, empyema, tumor in the paravertebral space; caution with coagulopathy, kyphoscoliosis or previous thoracic surgery
tips: Scout scan first to measure the depth to the transverse process and pleura
Use Doppler to find the intercostal vessels

art.caption: Transverse view beside a thoracic transverse process: local anesthetic in the wedge above the pleura.

blocks.name: Intercostal nerve block
blocks.summary: One nerve per level: rib fractures, chest and upper abdominal incisions.
indications: Rib fractures
Pain after chest and upper abdominal surgery
Herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia
coverage: The skin and muscles of each segment injected
blocks.position: Not stated on NYSORA's free pages
blocks.equipment: Not stated on NYSORA's free pages
blocks.target: Probe sagittal oblique across two ribs, at or just lateral to the rib angle (about 6–7.5 cm from the spinous process), counting up from the 12th rib. Needle in plane or out of plane through the external and internal intercostals, stopping just under the internal intercostal, above the pleura
volume: 3–5 mL per level
cautions: Keep the tip above the parietal pleura
NYSORA's free pages do not discuss pneumothorax or the high systemic absorption after intercostal injection
tips: Identify the gliding pleural line before advancing

art.caption: Sagittal view across two ribs: injection under the internal intercostal muscle, above the pleura.

blocks.name: Spinal anesthesia
blocks.summary: Technique and drug table; levels and doses by operation are in the Neuraxial Guide.
indications: Lower abdominal, perineal and lower-limb surgery; cesarean delivery (see the Neuraxial Guide for the level each needs)
coverage: Set by the drug's baricity, dose and the patient's position: hyperbaric solutions follow gravity, isobaric spread little with position
blocks.position: Lateral, sitting (saddle blocks, obese patients) or prone jackknife (hypobaric or isobaric solution)
blocks.equipment: Pencil-point needles (Whitacre, Sprotte) lower the risk of headache; an introducer for small-gauge needles
blocks.target: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (the iliac crests are usually at the L4 spinous process); conventionally never at or above the conus, which may lie anywhere from T12 to L3
volume: Bupivacaine 0.75%: 8–12 mg to T10, 14–20 mg to T4 (NYSORA Table 8; not for cesarean, which uses 8–12 mg by height)
Full drug table and procedure doses: Neuraxial Guide
cautions: Absolute contraindications: refusal, infection at the site, uncorrected hypovolemia, allergy, raised intracranial pressure
Relative: coagulopathy, sepsis, fixed cardiac output, indeterminate neurologic disease
tips: Tuffier's line often crosses one or two levels higher than expected; ultrasound identifies the interspace far better than palpation (about 30% correct by palpation)

art.caption: Lumbar interspace below the conus: L3–L4 or L4–L5.

blocks.name: Epidural anesthesia and analgesia
blocks.summary: Insertion by the incision's center; test dose; labor and cesarean dosing.
indications: Labor analgesia and cesarean delivery
Thoracic epidural with general anesthesia for thoracic and abdominal surgery; lumbar for lower-limb and vascular surgery
coverage: Segmental: the level depends on where the catheter sits and the volume given
blocks.position: Sitting or lateral; paramedian approach above T11, midline below (StatPearls)
blocks.equipment: Tuohy needle (17–18-gauge); loss of resistance to air, saline or both; about 5–6 cm of catheter left in the space (StatPearls)
blocks.target: Insertion: L3–L4 for labor and lower-limb surgery; T9–T11 for lower abdominal surgery; midthoracic for upper abdominal surgery; T2–T4 for breast surgery (NYSORA epidural chapter). The skin-to-space distance is about 4 cm in half of adults and 4–6 cm in 80%
volume: Test dose: 3 mL lidocaine 1.5% with epinephrine 1:200,000 (45 mg + 15 mcg)
Cesarean: 15–25 mL in divided doses; labor: 5–10 mL of 0.125–0.25% to start, then 8–12 mL/h of 0.0625–0.1%
NYSORA's open pages print no surgical regimen for other operations
cautions: Intravascular epinephrine 15 mcg raises the heart rate 20–30 beats/min within 30 seconds
A large volume in the cervical region can produce a subdural block

art.caption: Insertion by the center of the incision: lumbar for labor and the legs, thoracic for the chest and abdomen.

blocks.name: Caudal block (children)
blocks.summary: Children's sacral to lower thoracic blocks: circumcision, anal surgery, hernia repair.
indications: Children: circumcision and anal surgery (sacral), inguinal hernia repair (lower thoracic)
Adults: perineal, anal and lower-limb surgery, labor and chronic pain (less common)
coverage: Sacral to thoracic, set by the volume (about 0.1 mL per segment per year of age)
blocks.position: Children lateral (usually under general anesthesia); adults prone
blocks.equipment: Children: 21-gauge 1-inch short-bevel needle. Low-frequency curved probe, transverse across the cornua, then sagittal
blocks.target: The sacral hiatus between the two sacral cornua; feel the 'pop' through the sacrococcygeal ligament, flatten the needle and keep the tip below S2
volume: 1 mL/kg of bupivacaine 0.25% or ropivacaine 0.2%; or 2 mg/kg; or about 0.1 mL per segment per year (NYSORA's listed schemes)
Additives in pediatric studies: clonidine 2 mcg/kg, dexmedetomidine 1–2 mcg/kg
blocks.onset: Children: onset about 8–13 minutes, duration about 250–520 minutes for some agents
cautions: Use an epinephrine test dose: a heart-rate rise above 10 beats/min or a systolic rise above 15 mmHg suggests intravascular injection
Intraosseous or intravascular injection is absorbed fast: toxicity risk is higher than with lumbar or thoracic epidurals
Dural puncture if the needle or catheter is pushed above S2

art.caption: Sagittal view of the sacral hiatus: through the sacrococcygeal ligament into the caudal canal.

blocks.note: Carotid endarterectomy, superficial neck surgery, thyroidectomy

neck.note: The deep cervical plexus block is an advanced block (vertebral artery and intrathecal injection).

blocks.note: Shoulder surgery; most patients get hemidiaphragmatic paresis
Phrenic palsy less likely than interscalene, not avoidable
Away from the pleura and phrenic nerve
Hand and fingers only; an upper-arm tourniquet is not covered

neuraxial.text: Catheter at T2–T4; segmental T1–T7 for partial mastectomy, C5–T7 for modified radical mastectomy (NYSORA epidural Table 9).

blocks.note: Breast surgery; PECS II for mastectomy and axillary work

neuraxial.text: Segmental T1–T10 covers a thoracotomy incision and the chest-tube site (NYSORA).

blocks.note: Rib fractures, one level per injection
Back surgery: bilateral injections at the operative levels

neuraxial.text: Segmental T5 (T4 laparoscopic) to T8; NYSORA does not advise spinal as the only technique for these operations.

blocks.note: Subcostal approach for upper abdominal incisions
Posterior or transmuscular: incisions up to T6

neuraxial.text: T6 for intestinal, gynecologic and urologic surgery; cesarean needs T4. Epidural catheter between T9 and T11 (NYSORA).
NYSORA mentions spinal for lumbar procedures done prone, with a hypobaric or isobaric solution; it gives no level.
NYSORA prints no level for hernia repair; the incision lies at its T12 landmark (the inguinal ligament).
Sitting, hyperbaric solution, seated at least 5 minutes; prone jackknife cases take a hypobaric or isobaric solution.
T10 for hip surgery (spinal Table 5, epidural Table 2).

blocks.note: Hip fracture analgesia; weakens the quadriceps

neuraxial.text: T12 for femur fixation (epidural Table 2); spinal Table 5 gives L1 for thigh surgery; T10 suffices for most lower-limb operations.
Epidural Table 2: T12, T8 with a tourniquet; NYSORA adds that T10 from L3–L4 suits most lower-limb operations.

blocks.note: Front of the knee, largely quadriceps-sparing
Back of the knee, with the adductor canal block

neuraxial.text: T12 for tibia fixation and amputation (T8 with a tourniquet) in epidural Table 2.

blocks.note: Below the knee except the medial side

neuraxial.text: Epidural Table 2: T12 for the distal tibia, ankle and foot; spinal Table 5 gives L2.

blocks.note: Forefoot and toes, no calf weakness

procedures.name: Cesarean delivery
procedures.levelText: At least T4 (obstetric chapter; T3–T4 in its preeclampsia section). Visceral discomfort can occur even with an adequate level.
technique: Spinal is the most common technique, for its speed of onset and reliability
Epidural: top up an existing labor epidural
Combined spinal–epidural is also described
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
Epidural: lumbar; L3–L4 is the most common interspace in labor
spinal: Hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.75% in 8.25% dextrose, by height: 150–160 cm 8 mg; 160–180 cm 10 mg; over 180 cm 12 mg (obstetric Table 3)
Isobaric bupivacaine 0.5%: 8 mg; 10–12.5 mg; 12.5–15 mg for the same heights. Onset 2–4 min hyperbaric, 5–10 min isobaric
epidural: 15–25 mL in divided doses: lidocaine 2% with epinephrine 1:200,000, chloroprocaine 3% (rapid onset) or bupivacaine 0.5% (profound, slower); fractionating the dose is critical
adjuvants: Intrathecal: fentanyl 20 mcg or preservative-free morphine 0.1 mg (0.1–0.25 mg gives significant analgesia)
PROSPECT 2026 (NYSORA summary): intrathecal morphine 50–100 mcg or diamorphine 300 mcg, with regular paracetamol and NSAIDs
Epidural top-up: fentanyl 100 mcg or diamorphine 2.5–5 mg
notes: Hypotension: ephedrine 5–15 mg or phenylephrine 25–50 mcg IV, in increments (obstetric chapter; its complications section says ephedrine 5–10 mg)
The general spinal table's ‘to T4’ doses (bupivacaine 14–20 mg) are not obstetric doses; use the obstetric table above

procedures.name: Labor analgesia
procedures.levelText: T10–L1 for the first stage; S2–S4 added for the second stage (epidural chapter).
technique: Epidural or combined spinal–epidural
A single-shot spinal may need repeating in a long labor, which raises the risk of headache
insertion: Epidural: L3–L4, the most common interspace in labor
CSE: L3/L4 or below; a 27-gauge spinal needle (obstetric chapter)
spinal: CSE intrathecal dose: fentanyl 10–25 mcg or sufentanil 2.5–5 mcg, with or without up to 1 mL isobaric bupivacaine 0.25% (obstetric chapter)
epidural: Start: 5–10 mL bupivacaine, ropivacaine or levobupivacaine 0.125–0.25%
Maintain: 8–12 mL/h bupivacaine or levobupivacaine 0.0625%, or ropivacaine 0.1%
PCEA: 8 mL demand bolus, 10-minute lockout, with the infusion
Delivery: perineum with 10 mL bupivacaine 0.5% or lidocaine 1% (chloroprocaine 2% for rapid onset)
adjuvants: Epidural fentanyl 1–2 mcg/mL or sufentanil 0.3–0.5 mcg/mL
notes: Test dose: 3 mL lidocaine 1.5% with epinephrine 1:200,000 (45 mg + 15 mcg). Intravascular epinephrine 15 mcg raises the heart rate 20–30 beats/min within 30 seconds; give it between contractions
NYSORA pages differ on intrathecal sufentanil (2.5–5 mcg in the text, 5–10 mcg in a tip; most now use 2.5 or 5 mcg)

procedures.name: Anal and perineal surgery
procedures.levelText: S2 to S5: a saddle block (spinal Table 5).
technique: Saddle block: sitting, hyperbaric solution, the patient stays seated at least 5 minutes after injection
Prone jackknife cases: hypobaric or isobaric solution, to keep the block from spreading up
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
spinal: Procaine 50–100 mg is the only dose NYSORA prints for this range (perineal and lower-limb surgery); it prints no bupivacaine or lidocaine saddle dose
epidural: NYSORA lists anorectal surgery among ambulatory epidural uses; no regimen is printed

procedures.name: TURP and cystoscopy
procedures.levelText: TURP: T10 (spinal Table 5). The epidural chapter gives T9 for TURP and cystoscopy.
technique: Regional anesthesia is preferred to general for TURP: a change in mental status (TURP syndrome) and pain from a capsular or bladder perforation are noticed earlier, with less blood loss, fewer DVTs and less circulatory overload (epidural Table 4)
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
spinal: Spinal Table 8, to T10: bupivacaine 0.75% 8–12 mg; lidocaine 5% 50–75 mg, tetracaine 6–10 mg, ropivacaine 0.75% 15–17 mg, levobupivacaine 0.5% 10–15 mg, chloroprocaine 3% 30 mg. NYSORA prints no dose for this operation itself

procedures.name: Appendectomy
procedures.levelText: NYSORA names no appendectomy level; its nearest row is intestinal, gynecologic and urologic surgery, T6 (spinal Table 5).
technique: Epidural or combined spinal–epidural are described for lower abdominal procedures, appendectomy included
insertion: Epidural catheter between T9 and T11
spinal: One CSE study (laparoscopic appendectomy): spinal at L2–L3, hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% 2 mL (10 mg) with fentanyl 25 mcg; epidural catheter at T10–T11. A single study, not a NYSORA recommendation

procedures.name: Lower abdominal laparotomy, colectomy
procedures.levelText: T6 for intestinal, gynecologic and urologic surgery (spinal Table 5); the epidural chapter gives T7 or T9 for most colonic surgery.
technique: Thoracic epidural analgesia with general anesthesia: colectomy, bowel resection, abdominoperineal resection, hysterectomy (epidural Table 8)
insertion: Epidural catheter between T9 and T11 for lower abdominal surgery
spinal: The spinal table has no T6 column; NYSORA prints no spinal dose for this level
epidural: No surgical epidural regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages

procedures.name: Upper abdominal surgery
procedures.levelText: Segmental block from T5 (T4 for laparoscopic surgery) to T8 (epidural chapter); T4 for upper abdominal surgery (spinal Table 5).
technique: Midthoracic epidural with general anesthesia: esophagectomy, gastrectomy, pancreatectomy, hepatic resection, cholecystectomy (epidural Table 8)
insertion: Midthoracic; NYSORA prints no exact interspace
spinal: NYSORA does not recommend spinal as the only technique for these operations
epidural: No surgical epidural regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages

procedures.name: Hip arthroplasty, hip fracture
technique: Spinal or epidural. For hip fracture, a review cited in the spinal chapter found consistent benefit from spinal and recommended regional anesthesia whenever possible
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
Epidural: L3–L4 (T10 from L3–L4 suffices for most lower-limb orthopedic surgery)
Elderly: L5–S1 is typically the largest interspace (NYSORA tip)
spinal: Spinal Table 8, to T10: bupivacaine 0.75% 8–12 mg; lidocaine 5% 50–75 mg, tetracaine 6–10 mg, ropivacaine 0.75% 15–17 mg, levobupivacaine 0.5% 10–15 mg, chloroprocaine 3% 30 mg. NYSORA prints no dose for this operation itself
Elderly hip arthroplasty study (NYSORA elderly chapter): bupivacaine 15 mg with intrathecal morphine 50, 100 or 200 mcg; 100 mcg gave the best balance
adjuvants: Intrathecal morphine below 200 mcg can be a useful adjunct in the elderly (NYSORA elderly chapter)
epidural: No surgical epidural regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages

procedures.name: Knee arthroplasty
procedures.levelText: Epidural Table 2: T12, or T8 with a tourniquet; NYSORA adds that T10 from L3–L4 is adequate for most lower-limb orthopedic procedures.
technique: General and neuraxial anesthesia are both accepted; spinal is commonly preferred (observational evidence)
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
Epidural: L3–L4
spinal: Hyperbaric prilocaine 2% for operations up to about 90 minutes; bupivacaine or levobupivacaine for longer ones (no mg dose printed)

Spinal Table 8, to T10: bupivacaine 0.75% 8–12 mg; lidocaine 5% 50–75 mg, tetracaine 6–10 mg, ropivacaine 0.75% 15–17 mg, levobupivacaine 0.5% 10–15 mg, chloroprocaine 3% 30 mg. NYSORA prints no dose for this operation itself
adjuvants: Intrathecal morphine 100 mcg may be considered in selected patients
notes: Adductor canal and IPACK blocks are the usual peripheral partners: see Peripheral Nerve Blocks

procedures.name: Foot and ankle surgery
procedures.levelText: Epidural Table 2: T12 for distal tibia, ankle and foot; spinal Table 5 prints L2. With a thigh tourniquet NYSORA gives T8 for knee procedures and amputations.
technique: Spinal or epidural; foot surgery is among NYSORA's ambulatory epidural uses
Popliteal sciatic and saphenous or ankle blocks are the peripheral alternative: see Peripheral Nerve Blocks
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
Epidural: L3–L4
spinal: Procaine 50–100 mg (perineal and lower-limb surgery). The spinal table has no column for this level

procedures.name: Lower-limb vascular surgery, amputation
procedures.levelText: Epidural: T8–T10, reached by slow titration (vascular surgery). Spinal Table 5: L1 for thigh surgery and lower-leg amputation; epidural Table 2: T12, or T8 with a tourniquet, for amputation.
technique: Epidural for infrainguinal bypass, embolectomy, thrombectomy and endovascular procedures; spinal is also used
insertion: Spinal: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (spinal chapter); L3–L4 or below (CSE chapter)
Epidural: L3–L4 for lower-limb surgery
spinal: Spinal Table 8, to T10: bupivacaine 0.75% 8–12 mg; lidocaine 5% 50–75 mg, tetracaine 6–10 mg, ropivacaine 0.75% 15–17 mg, levobupivacaine 0.5% 10–15 mg, chloroprocaine 3% 30 mg. NYSORA prints no dose for this operation itself
epidural: Titrate slowly to T8–T10 while keeping the hemodynamics stable

procedures.name: Thoracotomy, VATS
procedures.levelText: A segmental block from T1 to T10 covers the incision and the chest-tube site (epidural chapter).
technique: Thoracic epidural with general anesthesia: thoracotomy, VATS, thymectomy, pectus repair, thoracic aneurysm repair (epidural Table 8)
Paravertebral and erector spinae blocks are the peripheral alternatives: see Peripheral Nerve Blocks
insertion: Thoracic; the insertion level is in a NYSORA figure, not its text (one VATS study placed catheters at T5–T7)
spinal: Intrathecal morphine 5 mcg/kg (ideal body weight) in one VATS study summarized by NYSORA; not a chapter recommendation
epidural: No regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages

procedures.name: Breast surgery
procedures.levelText: Segmental: T1–T7 for partial mastectomy or augmentation; C5–T7 for modified radical mastectomy; C5–L1 with a TRAM flap (epidural Table 9).
technique: Thoracic epidural
PECS, serratus anterior and paravertebral blocks are the peripheral alternatives: see Peripheral Nerve Blocks
insertion: Epidural T2–T4; T8–T10 for TRAM flap reconstruction
epidural: No regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages

procedures.name: Nephrectomy
procedures.levelText: T6 with a midthoracic catheter (radical nephrectomy); epidural Table 5 advises combined general–epidural anesthesia.
technique: Combined general–epidural anesthesia
insertion: Midthoracic; NYSORA prints no exact interspace
epidural: No regimen is printed on NYSORA's open pages
